explain.say: An airliner cruises at around 850 kilometres per hour but lands at about 250. Its wing is shaped for fast cruising, so for landing it changes shape by sliding out flaps and slats.

faq.a: Flaps are panels at the back of the wing that slide out and tilt down. They make the wing larger and more curved, giving more lift at low speed for take-off and landing.
asks: What are the flaps on a plane wing?
Why do the wings move before landing?

faq.a: Slats are panels on the front edge of the wing that slide forward, opening a narrow slot. Air through the slot keeps the flow smooth over the wing at high angles, so the wing can fly slower before it stalls.
asks: What is the front part of the wing that slides out?

faq.q: Why do planes need flaps to land?
faq.a: Without flaps an airliner would have to land much faster, needing a far longer runway and harder braking. Flaps let it touch down at a slower, safer speed.
asks: Could a plane land without flaps?

faq.a: A stall happens when the wing meets the air at too steep an angle and the smooth airflow breaks away from the top surface, so lift drops suddenly. It has nothing to do with the engine stopping.
asks: Does a stall mean the engine stops?

faq.a: Spoilers are panels on top of the wing that flip up. In flight they add drag and cut lift to slow down or descend; after touchdown they rise fully to dump lift, putting the plane's weight on the wheels for braking.
asks: What are the panels that pop up on the wing after landing?

facts: Lift grows with the square of speed, so halving speed cuts lift to a quarter unless the wing changes shape or angle.
Airliners typically take off and land at roughly 240 to 330 kilometres per hour.
